title: The Experience of Crowding: A Two-Factor Theory
research_question: Does the experience of crowding occur in a two-step process involving arousal from personal space violations and subsequent attribution of that arousal to other people, and can this experience be alleviated by distracting individuals from making this attribution?

participants.description: Male introductory psychology students, run in groups of 7 or 8 previously unacquainted subjects, University of Virginia.
participants.recruitment: Participated in a study entitled "group performance" in partial fulfillment of a course requirement.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Experimental rooms varied in size (low density: 20'6" x 11'6"; high density: 12'6" x 9"). Chairs arranged in a circle, varying interaction distance (close: chairs touching; far: 19.5 inches between chairs). Walls were either bare or had 6 prints and 2 wind chimes (attribution inhibitors).

measures.instrument: Composite rating of 4 self-report questions: comfortable, confined, ill at ease, and crowded (1=least crowded, 10=most crowded).
Self-report: estimated duration of 10-minute word game task.
Self-report: estimated duration of 20-minute Johnny Rocco case task.
Self-report: "Was there a leader or leaders in the group?"
Behavioral: number of group members' names recalled.
Self-report: "how pleasant they found the experimental room" (1=not at all pleasant, 10=very pleasant).
Self-report: "how distracted they found themselves during the experiment" (1=not at all distracted, 10=very distracted).
Behavioral: number of words formed from 'industriously'.
Self-report: individual recommendation for Johnny Rocco case (1=most benign, 7=most punitive).
Self-report: group consensus recommendation for Johnny Rocco case (1=most benign, 7=most punitive).
Composite rating of "How much did you like the people in your group?" and friendly ratings (1=not friendly, 10=friendly).
Self-report: rating of other members' nervousness (1=calm, 10=nervous).
Self-report: rating of other members' aggressiveness (1=passive, 10=aggressive).

mechanisms: Crowding is a two-step process: arousal from personal space violation, followed by attribution of that arousal to other people in the environment.

Attribution inhibitors (e.g., pictures) can divert attention from other people, preventing the attribution of arousal to them, thereby reducing the experience of crowding and associated negative effects.
moderators: Interaction Distance (moderates the effect of density and pictures)
Density (moderates the effect of interaction distance on aggressiveness attribution)
implementation_implications: To reduce crowding and associated negative behaviors, focus on maintaining appropriate personal interaction distances rather than simply reducing overall density.

In situations where close interaction is unavoidable, introducing 'attribution inhibitors' such as interesting visual stimuli (pictures) can alleviate the experience of crowding and its negative consequences.
Architectural design should consider personal space requirements, which vary by gender, task, and culture, to minimize stress and punitiveness.
In settings like juries, close interaction distances may lead to more punitive decisions, suggesting spatial arrangements can influence judicial outcomes.

limitations: Only male subjects were run, limiting generalizability to females, although the theory predicts similar results with a closer interaction distance for females.
The high-density (small) room was still large enough to allow some movement by subjects, which might have attenuated density effects.
The number of pictures used was chosen to avoid clutter; using many more pictures might lead to an increment rather than decrement in crowding.
